title: Deion Sanders Confused Over Travis Hunter’s Role: “I Have No Idea What’s Going On”
body:
Colorado head coach Deion Sanders has publicly voiced his frustration over the lack of communication from the Jacksonville Jaguars regarding the development and utilization of former five‑star recruit Travis Hunter. The former NFL star‑turned‑college coach, who is now overseeing the Colorado Buffaloes, said he “has no idea what’s going on” with the former Jaguars cornerback‑wide receiver, a situation that has raised questions about the player’s role on the Buffaloes and the broader coordination between NFL franchises and collegiate programs.

Sanders first raised the issue in May, noting that despite multiple attempts to reach out, the Jaguars had not provided any guidance on how best to coach or deploy Hunter, who arrived in Boulder after spending two seasons on Jacksonville’s roster. “I’ve reached out, I’ve sent emails, I’ve called. Nothing. I have no idea what they’re doing with him, what they expect,” Sanders said in a recent press conference. The lack of clarity has forced the Colorado coaching staff to make on‑the‑fly decisions about where to line up the 6‑4, 215‑pound athlete, who possesses the rare combination of size, speed, and ball‑handling ability that could make him a game‑changing weapon at either cornerback or wide receiver.

The communication gap is especially puzzling given the increasingly collaborative relationship between NFL teams and college programs when it comes to player development. In recent years, franchises have been more proactive in sharing scouting reports, conditioning programs, and positional drills to ensure that prospects who return to school continue to progress in a manner consistent with professional expectations. The Jaguars’ silence, therefore, not only hampers Colorado’s strategic planning but also potentially stalls Hunter’s own growth. Without clear direction, the Buffaloes risk misusing a talent that could otherwise become a marquee player in the Pac‑12.

From a tactical standpoint, the uncertainty has already manifested on the field. In the first two games of the season, Hunter has been shuffled between the secondary and the slot, resulting in limited snaps at either position. While his athleticism is evident—he recorded a 4.38‑second 40‑yard dash at the NFL combine and demonstrated reliable hands in practice—his lack of a defined role has prevented him from establishing rhythm and chemistry with teammates. Colorado’s offensive coordinator, Brian Lindgren, acknowledged that the coaching staff is “trying to find the sweet spot” but admitted that “without external input, we’re essentially guessing.”

Analysts suggest that the situation could have broader implications for recruiting. Prospective high‑school athletes watch how programs handle elite talent, especially when that talent has already experienced the professional ranks. If Colorado is perceived as unable to secure clear development pathways, it may deter future top‑tier recruits who seek assurance that their transition between college and the NFL will be managed effectively. Conversely, a successful resolution—whether through a formal agreement with Jacksonville or an internal consensus—could showcase the program’s adaptability and reinforce Sanders’ reputation for turning challenges into opportunities.

Looking ahead, the Buffaloes are expected to convene a meeting with the Jaguars’ front office within the next few weeks, aiming to establish a collaborative framework for Hunter’s usage. Sanders has hinted that a “mutual understanding” will allow Colorado to maximize the player’s impact while aligning with Jacksonville’s long‑term vision for him. As the season progresses, the clarity of that partnership will likely be reflected in Hunter’s snap counts, statistical output, and the overall performance of Colorado’s defense and offense. If the two organizations can bridge the communication gap, Travis Hunter could finally emerge as the versatile playmaker both his coaches and fans anticipate.
